parakeet: Because moral superiority is not just something other people have. It's a temptation inside every human community. And it thrives because it gives us psychological rewards. It gives us certainty in a complicated world. It gives us belonging inside a group. It gives us a villain to focus on, a sense of control, a story where we're the hero. And sometimes it gives us an escape from self-examination. Because if the problem is always those people, then I never have to look at myself. And that may be the most addictive part of moral superiority. It allows me to feel morally awake while remaining personally unexamined. One of the most dangerous ways moral superiority operates is through purity testing. A purity test happens when belonging to a group is no longer based on shared values, shared goals, or shared responsibility, but on constant proof that you're loyal enough, angry enough, extreme enough, obedient enough, or publicly aligned enough. It's not enough to care about the issue. You have to care in the approved language. You have to condemn the approved enemies. You have to share the approved outrage. You have to reject the approved people. You have to prove over and over again that you're still one of us. And this is where moral superiority becomes a loyalty weapon. Because once a group believes it occupies the morally superior position, disagreement is no longer treated as disagreement. Questions become betrayal, nuance becomes witness, compassion becomes complicity, boundaries, abandonment. And anyone who refuses to perform loyalty the expected way can be recast as unsafe, compromised, cowardly, or secretly aligned with the enemy.
